title: Awe walks
hookLine: in a study, older adults who took weekly "awe walks" reported more joy (Sturm et al.)

cards: Arm out, phone up, a quick selfie at the start of a walk. Again halfway. Again at the end.
Week after week, a group of older adults did exactly this for a research team. The walks were short. Nobody climbed anything.
When the researchers later laid the photos side by side, something had shifted in one group's pictures. The people in them took up less of the frame, and their smiles had changed.
That group had been given one small extra instruction before they set out.

teach.b: The study comes from Virginia Sturm and her colleagues. First, the setup. Everyone walked.
One group just walked. The other was asked to take an awe walk: to go with fresh eyes, as if seeing things for the first time, and to notice what was vast and what was small.
A cloud bank, a stretch of sky, the pattern on a leaf. Same legs, same shoes; only the attention changed. Second, what the awe walkers reported.
More awe, as you'd expect, but also more joy and more of the warm, outward feelings like gratitude and compassion, gains the researchers reported growing over the weeks. Third, the photos.

teach.h: A SMALLER SELF IN THE FRAME.
teach.b: In the awe group, people took up less of their own selfies as time went on: more sky, more trees, a little less self. Researchers call this the small self, the sense that you're one part of something larger.
And the smiles grew stronger. Smaller, and happier, at the same time. Fourth, a walker from long before would have recognized this.
Henry David Thoreau wrote an essay simply called Walking.
He opens with the word saunter, and offers two playful stories of where it came from: wanderers heading to the Holy Land, or people with no particular home, at home everywhere.

For Thoreau, even the shortest walk could be taken in a spirit of adventure. The study and the essayist land in the same place: you don't need a mountain, just a different kind of looking, on the block you already know.

how: People who take awe walks go on ordinary walks with the intention of noticing vast and tiny things with fresh eyes; some walk the same route regularly, and some take a photo along the way.

o: ordinary walks taken with fresh eyes, noticing the vast and the small
silent walks done in a group, following a trained guide's lead
long hikes to well-known views, like canyons, peaks and waterfalls

games.q: you're in the study. you've been told to take an awe walk this week. what changes?
o: you walk the same, but look with fresh eyes.
you walk somewhere you've never been.
games.why: same legs, same shoes. the awe walkers were asked to notice the vast and the small, as if for the first time.

practice: Walk slowly around the room or out a door, or, if you can't, let your eyes do the walking out the nearest window, with the awe walk's one instruction: fresh eyes.
Find one thing that is vast, a sky, a ceiling, a long view, then one thing that is tiny, a crack, a thread, a leaf. Go back and forth between them, and let yourself be small for a minute.

wordCard.voice: Awe walks. Ordinary walks taken with fresh eyes, noticing the vast and the small. In one study, the walkers reported more joy. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: awe walk. Same route, fresh eyes, a smaller self in the frame. Rest well.
